Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

btw @karpathy uses medium on opus 5.5 on his latest project (Hackertube launched today).

overall i think having strong opinions on effort levels is like the tabs vs spaces of our time. just tweak to taste. altho mine is definitely superior to yours. https://t.co/oSCPvlogKc

In updating a graphic showing U.S. company AI adoption over time according to a long-running U.S. Census Bureau survey, I found out that the Bureau's work has been sullied by that asinine "Super Intelligence" executive order https://t.co/YEu1tnWweT

Increasingly this will be the new job description for a lot of roles, not just coding. We’re clearly moving from a world where agents help us do our work incrementally better or faster, to us helping agents do their work.

This turns everyone in one of these positions to that of a manager of a team of agents, instead of an individual contributor with just some added leverage from AI. The biggest areas of impact will be information-heavy jobs, like coding, cybersecurity, legal work, biotech, engineering, and many other fields. 

And as a result, in these jobs your leverage will begin to be decoupled from the normal ratio of hours spent working to output generated. For essentially the history of knowledge work the main variable you had to play with was hours of work done (assuming fixed level talent/coordination/strategy). 

Now we’ve separated these variables because agents can parallelize work for us, to in theory execute as much as we need to pull off whatever goal we’re trying to accomplish. The people and organizations that discover this sooner, and orient their operations around it, will see compounding gains in their workflows.

Did you know the same intelligence can cost 10× more, need 6× more output tokens and take twice as long?

In addition to task spend, Agent Arena now shows which agents give you best performance for every output token generated and every minute you wait.

These real-world usage plots reveal that costs grow most steeply with intelligence, waiting longer pays off unevenly, and output tokens barely predict the bill.

To find the best model for you, see the link in thread.

The top 10 agents in Agent Arena process about 93 input tokens for every token they generate, according to our analysis of 26K+ sessions.

This is why labs are racing to lower the cost of cached input.

Dive into the details of the hidden AI price war: article by @DawidGalarowicz below.

We are collaborating with Silicon Data to bring market-based GPU pricing into AA-AgentPerf, our datacenter system performance benchmark

Our users and partners want to know how much agent work they can support per dollar of compute. @silicondata's rental price indices allow us to report a reliable value-for-money metric, updated daily as prices change. We currently display Silicon Data indices for H100, H200, B200 and B300, tracked across cloud providers

The new metric is Throughput per $/hr, which divides the total throughput of a system and serving configuration by the hourly cost of renting that system. Among systems with available rental pricing, NVIDIA’s B300 generally leads, while B200 matches it at faster output speeds on some models

Note: the below chart includes an MI355X rental rate that has been assumed by Artificial Analysis based on recent market quotes

I always cringe a little when people refer to me as an “expert” in ai policy. This field is too new, too thinly institutionalized, too pre-paradigmatic, to have any experts at all. We are on the open seas.

The positive side of this is that the field is wide open to people looking to make novel contributions. There is no grand literature to learn, no pantheon of elders to whom one must pay their dues.
